1.pericope_label: Let brotherly love continue; entertain strangers; remember them that are in bonds

schools.summary: Confine brotherly love to those in the same spiritual relation and church state, and make being brethren inseparable from being Christians; diagnose the occasion as Jewish haughtiness threatening to divide the churches; commend the entertaining of the needy rather than the hospitality of the rich, and answer the objection that angelic guests are rare by pointing to Christ received in the poor; and refer being in the body to the body of the Church rather than to shared human liability.

Distinguish the affection commanded from natural and familial affection; and identify the two things that endanger it, persecution and doctrinal dispute, the second producing a decay of Christian affection.

Explain hospitality from the absence of public inns; confine the remembrance of prisoners to those suffering for the testimony of Jesus; and read the closing clause of shared bodily liability to the same treatment.

Correct the rendering to the love of the brethren; argue from the verb that the love already existed and needed no reproof; restrict hospitality to Christian brethren from a distance and support it from the earliest patristic witness; locate the sense of the angel clause in the participle; and extend the remembrance of prisoners to every kind of captive, including the criminal and the enslaved.

debates: Who is meant by them that are in bonds: Gill and Clarke confine it to those imprisoned for the gospel, while Barnes extends it to prisoners of war, men held for trial, the criminal and the enslaved alike.

What “as being yourselves also in the body” means: shared human liability to suffering (Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott), being as it were in the sufferers’ own body, or membership of the body of the Church — Calvin reports the first two, rejects both, and holds the third.
Whether the command implies the love was intact or endangered: Barnes and Ellicott argue from the verb that it existed, Henry and Calvin name the forces then eroding it.
Whom hospitality is owed to — any stranger, the wicked not excepted (Gill), the needy and the fugitive (Calvin), or Christian brethren away from home (Ellicott).
outliers: Calvin alone turns the apostolic use of “brother” into a rebuke of the monastic orders of his own day.
Barnes alone applies the verse to the prisons of his own country and to slavery.
Calvin alone raises and answers the objection that entertaining angels is too rare an event to motivate anyone.
Robertson alone rests the sense of the clause on the supplementary participle rather than on the main verb.

4.pericope_label: Marriage honourable; the bed undefiled; freedom from covetousness; the Lord is my helper

schools.summary: Weigh the three possible constructions of the first clause and settle on marriage as the appointed remedy against fornication; list the marks of covetousness and the reason for warning these readers of it; trace covetousness to mistrust as its root; and decline to assign the promise to any single passage, taking it for the common doctrine of Scripture.

Note that the Greek supplies no copula and choose the imperative; set the precept against a false asceticism and against Gentile laxity and Jewish divorce; distinguish the two classes of offenders; observe the spread of the rare compound for freedom from avarice; and identify the promise as a free paraphrase of several passages, already current in that form.

Assert the honour of marriage for clergy and laity alike against both an ancient sect and a modern church, arguing from the proportion of the sexes in nature; report a variant reading that turns the clause into the reason of the prohibition; make covetousness the characteristic vice of old age; and hold that the apostle strengthened the wording of the old promise because the new covenant warrants more confidence.

debates: How the verbless first clause is to be construed — as assertion, as exhortation, or as concession; Calvin sets out all three and takes marriage as the remedy for fornication.

Where the promise “I will never leave thee” comes from: substantially the same words in three passages (Barnes), words spoken to Joshua and Solomon and deliberately strengthened by the apostle (Clarke), one passage though not in that exact form (Ellicott), a free paraphrase of four already current in that shape (Robertson), or no particular text at all but the common doctrine of Scripture (Calvin).
Whom the honour of marriage is asserted against — an ancient ascetic sect (Clarke) or the celibacy of the medieval and Roman clergy (Barnes, Wesley, Ellicott).

Whether the connecting particle is “but” or “for”, and so whether the second clause states a further command or the reason of the first — Clarke gives the manuscript evidence, Ellicott simply renders it “for”.
outliers: Barnes alone calls the doctrine of celibate purity the most harmful opinion ever to claim religious sanction.
Clarke alone argues the honour of marriage from the numerical proportion of the sexes, and alone names an ancient sect as the target.
Calvin alone identifies mistrust as the root from which covetousness grows.
Robertson alone cites a first-century Jewish writer to show the quotation was already circulating in the apostle’s wording.

7.pericope_label: Remember your leaders and imitate their faith; Jesus Christ the same; be not carried away by strange teachings

schools.summary: Take the leaders as teachers rather than rulers while noting the word shifts sense later in the chapter; read the closing noun as an exit from the world and deny that the following sentence can be construed as the aim of their living; treat the silence about martyrdom as deliberate; hinge the eighth verse between what precedes and follows; and adopt the better-attested verb in the ninth while cautioning that novelty is not by itself error.

Take the leaders as pastors and subordinate governors under Christ the King; extend “yesterday” back to the beginning of the world; deny that the verse concerns Christ’s essence rather than the knowledge of him held by the godly in every age; and trace all doctrinal error to a failure to abide in Christ alone.

Identify the dead leaders as martyrs on patristic authority; make “yesterday” the whole period in which access lay only through blood shed or typified; give the manuscript evidence for the stronger verb and gloss it as apostasy; and identify the “meats” as the Levitical sacrifices on which the offerers feasted.
Set the permanence of the great High Priest against the passing of the ministers, equally merciful and powerful under both dispensations.

debates: Whether the eighth verse asserts the divine immutability of Christ — Barnes calls it an irrefragable proof of his divinity, Calvin denies it speaks of his eternal existence at all and confines it to the constancy of the knowledge of him, “quality and not essence”.
Whether the leaders died as martyrs: asserted by Clarke on patristic authority, favoured but not pressed by Calvin, and read by Ellicott as something the writer deliberately declines to say.
Whether the word for leaders means teachers or rulers — Barnes distinguishes the two senses within the chapter, Gill takes the governing sense throughout.
How far back “yesterday” reaches: the days of Christ’s flesh (Robertson), the whole Old Testament dispensation (Calvin), or the beginning of the world (Gill).
Which verb the ninth verse carries, “carried about” or “carried away” — Clarke gives the evidence, Ellicott traces the weaker reading to a parallel epistle.
outliers: Barnes alone argues that a mutable Saviour would make Christian effort pointless.
Ellicott alone builds an argument on what the writer refrains from saying.
Robertson alone warns that the old is not right merely for being old.
Calvin alone turns the verse against the Roman handling of error, as a remedy that buries the knowledge of Christ.

10.pericope_label: We have an altar; the bodies burned without the camp; Jesus suffered without the gate

schools.summary: Deny that the altar is either the cross or the Lord’s table and identify it with Christ himself as altar, victim and priest; read the fittings of the old altar as figures; specify the two beasts of the day of atonement and match the rite step by step to the passion; and ground the exclusion on the one sacrifice of which the priests ate no part.

Take the altar as the cross or as a spiritual altar carried through in metaphor; explain the exclusion from the priests’ legal right of maintenance; correct the connecting particle to “moreover”; trace the custom from the camp to the city; and hold the gate and the camp to answer each other as what lies outside the dwelling-place of God’s people.

Put the altar for the sacrifice offered on it; report that the total consumption of the sin-offering showed sin was not pardoned by it; and read the suffering outside the gate as Christ’s abandonment of the city and the bringing in of the Gentiles.

debates: What the altar is: not the cross and not the Lord’s table but Christ himself (Gill), the cross (Barnes, Wesley), the sacrifice offered on it (Clarke), or a spiritual altar held deliberately abstract (Robertson).

Why those who serve the tabernacle may not eat — because the higher sacrifice is closed to them while they remain Jews (Barnes), or because the type itself gave the priests no portion of that particular victim (Calvin).
Whether the connecting particle introduces a reason or a fresh consideration — Barnes alone re-renders it.
What the burning outside the camp signified: that sin was not pardoned by such offerings (reported by Clarke), or simply the correspondence with Christ’s suffering outside the gate (Ellicott).
outliers: Barnes alone asks why the crucifixion took place outside the walls and answers from Roman judicial procedure, and alone denies that the traditional site can be genuine.
Clarke alone reads the departure from the city as a prophetic abandonment of it.
Robertson alone notes that the word used for the victims occurs nowhere else in either Testament in that sense.

13.pericope_label: Go forth unto him without the camp; here we have no continuing city; the sacrifice of praise and of doing good

schools.summary: Identify the camp with the Jewish dispensation and the city with a Jerusalem about to fall; produce a rabbinic maxim that all sacrifice but praise ceases in the days of the Messiah; note that the Greek and Hebrew of the prophetic quotation differ; and deny that reliance on Christ’s sacrifice avails in a man without charity to his neighbour.

Frame the departure as a choice between synagogue and church admitting no fellowship; draw from the fourteenth verse an argument that the letter predates the fall of Jerusalem; explain the sacrifice of praise from the peace-offering and the thank-offering; and observe that the New Testament’s definitions of worship are inward and ethical.

Read the camp as this world as well as the ceremonial system, and going forth as the weaning of the affections; set the cost of the departure in exiles and reproaches; treat frequent unsettlement as a mercy against the sloth bred by a quiet life; construe the prophetic quotation as apposition rather than construction; and make every act of love a sacrifice while calling the legal elements now positively harmful.
Measure the duty of beneficence by ability, to the necessities of the souls and bodies of men, and rest its acceptance on Christ.

debates: What the camp is that must be left: the Jewish dispensation (Wesley, Clarke, Robertson, Ellicott) or the world at large as well (Gill, Calvin).
Whether the fourteenth verse dates the epistle before the fall of Jerusalem — the inference is reported by Robertson, implied by Clarke’s seven or eight years, and left undrawn by Ellicott.

How the prophetic quotation stands to its Hebrew original: the Greek reading “fruit” against a Hebrew “heifers” (Clarke), a difference of expression only (Ellicott), or a question of apposition against construction settled by the Targum (Calvin).
Whether beneficence is a condition of acceptance or a fruit of it — Clarke denies that reliance on Christ avails without it, Barnes and Henry treat it as the offering of those already accepted.
outliers: Clarke alone enlists a rabbinic maxim to argue that the Jewish authorities themselves expected sacrifice to end.
Barnes alone turns the exhortation into a test of the reader’s own willingness to be reproached.
Calvin alone treats being often tossed about as a remedy for spiritual sloth, and alone calls the legal ceremonies positively harmful rather than merely obsolete.
Robertson alone remarks that all three New Testament definitions of worship are ethical rather than ritual.

17.pericope_label: Obey them that have the rule over you; pray for us; we trust we have a good conscience

schools.summary: Argue the command from the consequences of its absence — the chorus, the phalanx, the ship, the flock — and rank the evils, holding a wicked ruler worse than no ruler at all.

Classify what may lawfully be commanded and bound the obligation at conscience; render the second verb as yielding and note that it and the closing adjective occur nowhere else in the New Testament; press the emphasis on those who watch for souls; and report a variant that turns “we trust” into “we are persuaded”, inferring from the request itself that the writer was under suspicion in that church.

Deny that Jewish authorities or magistrates are meant, there being then no Christian magistrates; collect four renderings of the second verb and take it of a submissive mind rather than an outward act; and restrict the whole command to pastors who faithfully perform the office.

Limit the surrender to the will and to things indifferent, expressly excepting conscience and judgment; make the verse a test of the pastor as much as of the people; and account for the Church’s weakness by its want of prayer.
Build on the modesty of “we trust” rather than “we know”, against the Jewish suspicion of an apostle who had cast off the Levitical law.

debates: How far obedience extends: never to what is wrong in itself, with a threefold division of what may be commanded (Barnes); to the will only and in things indifferent, never to conscience or judgment (Wesley); only to pastors who faithfully discharge the office (Calvin); while Chrysostom holds a wicked ruler a worse evil than having none.
Whether the text reads “we trust” or “we are persuaded” — Henry draws a lesson in humility from the first, Ellicott reports the second as the better reading.
Whom the plural “us” includes — the rulers just named or the writer’s fellow labourers; Ellicott raises the question and leaves it open.
What the closing adjective means: simply unprofitable, or positively hurtful (Robertson).
outliers: Chrysostom alone ranks bad government as a worse evil than no government.
Clarke alone warns that faithful pastors will be obliged to accuse their own flocks before God.
Ellicott alone infers from the request for prayer that the writer’s motives were mistrusted by his readers.
Barnes alone makes a good conscience the condition of any right to ask the prayers of others.

20.pericope_label: The God of peace, that brought again from the dead the great Shepherd; make you perfect in every good work

schools.summary: Detach the clause about the blood from the raising and make the Shepherd great by that blood; trace the language to the Greek of Isaiah and to Zechariah, noting the epithet as the writer’s own and this as the letter’s only direct mention of the resurrection; infer the title “God of peace” from the divisions in the church; and deny that the prayer asserts any present or attainable perfection.

Take peace for prosperity of every kind; collect the prophetic titles of the Shepherd and explain the raising as the Father’s acceptance of the sacrifice; and expound the prayer as complete inward cleansing issuing in outward conformity, both wrought by the blood.

Render the preposition “in” and infer that Christ’s death retains its efficacy for ever; make the petition a doctrine of dependence, since we are unfit to do good until God forms us and perseverance is his peculiar gift; and measure a good work solely by the revealed will of God.
Read the descent and rising through the prophet in the fish, who cried out of the belly of hell and whose head went down to the chasms of the mountains, taken for the rock-hewn sepulchre.

debates: Where the clause about the blood belongs: Barnes refuses to attach it to the raising and asks what sense that could bear, making the Shepherd great by the blood, while Ellicott and Robertson attach it to the bringing up and Calvin reads the preposition as “in”.
Which prophecy supplies the title: three shepherd passages held in common (Clarke) or one text in its Greek form (Ellicott, Robertson).
How far the prayer for perfection reaches — Barnes denies it asserts perfection in this life, Clarke expounds it as cleansing from all sin issuing in outward conformity.
Whether the word rendered “make perfect” is the same the epistle uses elsewhere — Ellicott distinguishes two, one opposed to immaturity and one meaning full equipment.
outliers: Ellicott alone reasons from the writer’s usage elsewhere to the state of the church he is addressing.
Robertson alone observes that this is the only direct mention of the resurrection in the epistle.
Clarke alone explains why the raising is ascribed to the Father rather than the Son.
Cyril alone leaves the verse’s grammar aside for a typological reading of the descent into Hades.

22.pericope_label: Bear with the word of exhortation; our brother Timothy is set at liberty

schools.summary: Explain the entreaty by the writer’s standing with Jewish readers who resented his preaching down the ceremonies; take the notice of Timothy as a release from imprisonment; and read the mention of brevity as a guard against seeming to displace the ordinary preaching of pastors, Scripture not having been given to silence them.

Account for the entreaty by the offence the argument must have given; render the phrase simply as writing briefly and weigh it against the copiousness of the subject; deny on external evidence that Timothy was ever imprisoned and refer the notice to a mission; report the manuscript support for the possessive; and infer only that the writer, whoever he was, was then at liberty.

Deny that the letter is brief by comparison with the writer’s others and make the brevity relative to the difficulty of the subjects, or else to the time it would take to read aloud; note the idiom as unique in the New Testament; and take the familiar mention of Timothy as evidence of Pauline authorship.
Ground the need of entreaty not in the occasion but in human corruption, which resists even comfortable doctrine delivered with convincing evidence.

debates: Whether Timothy had been released from prison (Gill) or sent away on an errand (Barnes, Clarke), Clarke denying on external grounds that he was ever imprisoned at all.

Who wrote the epistle: Barnes takes the mention of Timothy as strong evidence for Paul, Clarke hedges between Paul and “the writer of this epistle”, and Ellicott elsewhere treats the author as a disciple of Paul.

In what sense the letter is “in few words” — brief against the difficulty of its subjects (Barnes, Wesley), brief as an hour’s reading (Ellicott), or a phrase not about length at all but about not supplanting the preaching of pastors (Calvin).
Why an entreaty was needed: the writer’s standing with these readers (Gill, Clarke) or the general resistance of men to being exhorted (Henry, Calvin).
outliers: Calvin alone reads the apology for brevity as a defence of the preaching office rather than a comment on the letter’s length.
Barnes alone remarks that this epistle cannot well be explained without a commentary longer than itself.
Clarke alone gives manuscript evidence for the possessive pronoun, and alone declines to identify the writer with Paul while arguing about his circumstances.

24.pericope_label: Salute all your leaders and all the saints; they of Italy salute you; grace be with you all

schools.summary: Ask why any should be greeted apart in a general letter and answer that the rulers are honoured in order to win their assent; offer two accounts of the saints named beside them; read the repeated “all” as deliberate universality; and expand the closing benediction into its particular blessings.

Take the greeting from Italy as fixing the place of writing, or refuse to decide between the two constructions it will bear; note without explanation that no names are given, contrary to the writer’s usual practice; and deny the closing subscription any authority, showing that its content is itself inferred from the last two verses.

Read the greeting as placing the writer in Italy after his release; trace the word “saint” from a real description to a mere title; and set the versions and manuscripts side by side to show how far their subscriptions disagree.

debates: What “they of Italy salute you” establishes: that the writer was in Italy and probably at Rome (Barnes, Clarke), or nothing at all, the phrase being equally consistent with his writing to Italy from elsewhere (Ellicott, Robertson).
Whether the closing subscription carries any weight — all three who mention it deny it, Ellicott showing that its statements about Rome and Timothy are themselves drawn from the two preceding verses.

Why particular persons are singled out for greeting in a letter addressed generally: Calvin takes it for a conciliatory move toward the leadership, while Barnes notes the absence of names and confesses the reason unknown.
Whom “all the saints” denotes — the Gentile believers, greeted so that both parties should learn unity, or simply the whole membership (Calvin offers the first, Gill and Clarke the second).
outliers: Calvin alone treats the salutation as a rhetorical manoeuvre designed to secure the rulers’ agreement.
Barnes alone records an omission that tells against the case for Pauline authorship he presses elsewhere in the chapter.
Ellicott alone dates the subscription and shows it to be an inference from the text rather than independent testimony.
Clarke alone assembles the competing subscriptions of the versions and manuscripts.
